domain: natural language processing / computational social science

paper_a.title: ChatGPT outperforms crowd workers for text-annotation tasks
paper_a.authors: Fabrizio Gilardi, Meysam Alizadeh, Maël Kubli

paper_b.title: Are chatbots reliable text annotators? Sometimes
paper_b.authors: Ross Deans Kristensen-McLachlan, Miceal Canavan, Márton Kardos, Mia Jacobsen, Lene Aarøe

conflicting_claim: ChatGPT can reliably replace human annotators and outperforms standard approaches on social science text annotation tasks.
evidence_a: Figure 1: Across 6,183 documents, ChatGPT's zero-shot accuracy exceeds MTurk crowd workers by ~25 percentage points on average, and its intercoder agreement exceeds both crowd workers and trained annotators across all tasks.
evidence_b: Results (Figures 1–2): Evaluated on 200 multi-coded US news tweets per task, GPT-3.5-turbo and GPT-4 show unpredictable prompt-dependent variance and low precision on the exemplar task (GPT-4 zero-shot recall dropping to 0.1), consistently underperforming a supervised DistilBERT classifier.
explanation: Gilardi et al. (2023) demonstrate that zero-shot ChatGPT outperforms MTurk crowd workers in accuracy and achieves higher intercoder agreement than human annotators across multiple text annotation tasks. Conversely, Kristensen-McLachlan et al. (2025) benchmark GPT-3.5-turbo, GPT-4, and open-source LLMs against human-coded tweets and supervised classifiers, finding brittle, prompt-sensitive performance—especially on nuanced concepts like exemplars—and advising researchers to rely on human labeling and supervised DistilBERT models instead.
